transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well… I hope it’s alright I came in. It’s a little embarrassing. At church, I’ve been doing some odd things, I guess. Like I’ll stand by the potluck table holding the serving spoon up and just… not move for a while. Or I’ll fold the same stack of napkins over and over, even when people are waiting on me. I don’t mean to be difficult.
When you keep folding the napkins over and over, does it feel like something bad will happen if you stop?

I don’t rightly know. I don’t think it’s like I’m thinking something terrible will happen, no… at least I haven’t noticed that. It’s more like I just get caught doing it, if that makes sense. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
When that happens, do you ever hear voices that other people can’t hear?

Voices? No… I don’t think so, Doctor. Not like somebody talking that nobody else hears. I mean, sometimes church is noisy and I may get mixed up, but I haven’t noticed voices like that. Is that… is that the right sort of answer?
When you get stuck holding still like that, can other people easily move you, or do you stay fixed in place?

I… I’m not sure about the moving me part, Doctor. I don’t think anyone’s really tried to move me. They’ll say my name or sort of wait, and then I notice I’m just standing there with the spoon up, looking foolish. It isn’t like I’m trying to make trouble. I just get stuck doing these odd things sometimes, like with the napkins too. Is that answering what you mean?
Since you were a child, have you usually found it hard to understand social cues or make back-and-forth conversation?

Oh… since I was a child? I don’t rightly know, Doctor. I don’t think anyone ever said that about me, not in those words. I was maybe a quiet girl, but… I got along well enough, I think. Conversation can be hard when I don’t know what someone wants from me, but I’m not sure if that’s what you mean. Is that alright to say?
Have there been times when you felt unusually energetic and needed much less sleep than usual?

No… I don’t think so, Doctor. I sleep about how I sleep, I suppose. I can get restless now and then, but not like being full of energy and not needing sleep. At least I haven’t noticed that. Is that what you mean?
Have these getting-stuck spells started after any medical illness or injury?
I don’t think so, Doctor. Not that I can remember, anyway. I haven’t had some big sickness or accident that I’d connect it to. It just… sort of happens. I’m sorry, I’m not sure if that’s helpful.
When you get stuck doing these things, do upsetting thoughts keep coming into your mind that you do not want?
I don’t know… I wouldn’t say it like that, Doctor. I don’t think it’s thoughts I don’t want coming in, not exactly. I just sort of… get stuck. Maybe I’m not explaining it right. Is that okay?
When you are folding the napkins over and over, does it make you feel less anxious?

I’m not sure, Doctor… I don’t think I do it to calm myself, exactly. Maybe it feels a little better when they’re neat, but I haven’t really noticed if it makes me less anxious. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
When you keep folding the napkins, does it feel wrong until they are arranged just right?

I’m not sure I’d say it feels wrong, Doctor… not exactly. I just keep fussing with them, I suppose. Sometimes I want them to look neat, but I haven’t really noticed a strong feeling like something bad or wrong until it’s just right. Is that answer okay?
As a child, did you often line up or sort objects over and over for long periods?

I don’t really remember doing that, Doctor. I mean, maybe I played with things like any child would, but lining them up over and over for a long time… I can’t say that I did. Is that what you’re asking?
Do you believe things that other people say are not true, even though they feel completely real to you?

I… I don’t know, Doctor. I don’t think so. Sometimes things can feel very real to me in the moment, but I’m not sure I’d say I believe things that aren’t true. Maybe I get mixed up sometimes, but… I wouldn’t want to say it wrong. Is that what you mean?
Do people ever have trouble understanding you because your thoughts or speech become hard to follow?

Well… maybe a little, Doctor. I don’t mean to be confusing on purpose. Sometimes when the ladies ask me something simple, like about the blankets or choir practice, I try to answer plain, but then my words sort of wander off… I’ll start talking about beans, then hymns, then my roses, and I can see by their faces they don’t quite know where I went.

It’s not all the time, I don’t think. But yes, I suppose people do have trouble following me sometimes. Is that the sort of thing you mean?
Have people told you that you seem to show very little emotion on your face or in your voice?

I don’t think anyone has said it to me that way, Doctor. At least… not that I remember. I try to be polite and answer when people talk to me. Maybe sometimes I’m quiet or tired-looking, but I haven’t noticed my face or voice being… empty like that. Is that alright to say?
When you are standing still with the spoon or folding the napkins again and again, does it feel like you have to do it even though you know it does not make sense?

Yes… I suppose so, Doctor. I don’t like to make a fuss about it, because it sounds silly when I say it.

At church, by the potluck table, I’ll sometimes just stand there holding the serving spoon up, not moving like I should. Or I’ll keep folding the same napkins again and again while people are waiting. I know it doesn’t help anything, and I know it must look odd… but in the moment I just sort of get stuck doing it. Is that what you mean?
Before you get stuck with the spoon or the napkins, do unwanted thoughts pop into your mind and push you to do it?

I… I don’t know that there’s a thought first, Doctor. Not like a clear one telling me, “Do this.” It’s more that I notice I’m already holding it, or already folding, and then I feel embarrassed because I should be moving along.

Maybe there’s a feeling of being stuck, but I can’t say there are unwanted thoughts pushing me. I hope that answers it right.
While you’re stuck with the spoon or folding the napkins, do you know at that moment that what you’re doing doesn’t make sense?

I think… yes, Doctor, at least part of me knows it doesn’t make good sense. Like at church, by the potluck table, I’ll be standing there with the serving spoon up, not really serving, or I’ll be folding the same napkins again while people are waiting.

I know that isn’t helpful, and I feel foolish about it. I don’t mean to hold everyone up. It just happens, and then I realize how odd it must look. Does that answer what you’re asking?
When you notice yourself stuck holding the spoon or folding the napkins, can you stop if you decide to?

I can sometimes, if I notice it and make myself… but it isn’t as easy as just deciding, “Stop now.” I get sort of caught there.

Like with the spoon at the church potluck, I’ll be standing there holding it up, and I know people are waiting, and I feel awful about it. Or with the napkins, I’ll realize I’ve folded the same little stack again and again. I can stop eventually, especially if someone says something or I feel embarrassed enough, but in the moment I don’t seem to move along like I should.

I’m sorry, I know that sounds strange. Is that what you mean?
When you start to get stuck with the spoon or the napkins, do you feel an inner urge to resist it or fight against doing it?

I don’t know if I’d call it an urge to fight it, Doctor. It’s more… I notice I’m doing it and I feel bad, like, “Oh no, I’m holding people up again.”

At church, by the potluck table, I’ll be standing there with the serving spoon up and not moving, or I’ll keep folding the same napkins while folks are waiting. I do want to stop because it looks odd and it’s not helpful, but it doesn’t feel like a strong fight inside so much as me getting stuck and then feeling embarrassed. Does that make sense?
If someone gently moves your arm while you’re stuck holding the spoon up, does your arm stay where they place it?

I’m not really sure, Doctor. I don’t think anyone has actually moved my arm like that, not that I remember.

What I do know is I’ll sort of get stuck there at the potluck table, holding the serving spoon up, or I’ll keep folding the same napkins over and over while people are waiting. But whether my arm would stay where someone put it… I’m sorry, I don’t know. Is that alright to say?

I’m not really sure, Doctor. I don’t think anyone has actually moved my arm like that, not that I remember.

What I do know is I’ll sort of get stuck there at the potluck table, holding the serving spoon up, or I’ll keep folding the same napkins over and over while people are waiting. But whether my arm would stay where someone put it… I’m sorry, I don’t know. Is that alright to say?

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes recurrent repetitive behaviors that she recognizes as senseless, feels embarrassed by, and can interrupt only with difficulty, which is most consistent with obsessive-compulsive disorder with mixed obsessional thoughts and acts despite poorly articulated obsessions. Schizophrenia/catatonic schizophrenia was considered because of getting 'stuck' and mildly tangential speech, but core psychotic symptoms were not established: she denied hallucinations, did not clearly endorse delusions, and catatonic features such as waxy flexibility were not confirmed.
